title: The Fantasy Behind Trump’s Anti-Smithsonian Crusade
author: @NewYorker
content:
Trump claims that the institution has fallen into the hands of Marxist radicals. A stroll through the exhibitions suggests otherwise.

August 20, 2026

The Immokalee Statue of Liberty in “Many Voices, One Nation,” at the National Museum of American History.Photograph by Lawren Simmons

Earlier this month, when I visited the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History (N.M.A.H.), President Trump’s signage warning of its “ideological capture” had yet to be installed. National Guardsmen marched in the paralyzing heat, which, along with the shadows cast by a revolving sculpture in the courtyard, suggested the eerie calm before the gunfight in a Western. Finally, the silence was broken by laughter—a group of volunteers from Citizen Historians for the Smithsonian, who’d advised me, via text, to look out for “4 old white ladies 🧓🏼🧑🏼‍🦳🧓🏼🧑🏼‍🦳”

“I just think what’s going on is a false narrative,” Deborah Greenbush, a D.C. tour guide who’s taken countless visitors through the museum, said. “I have never once had any adult or youngster express the feeling that what they saw made them feel bad. If it’s factual and actual, we should talk about it.” Next to her were Cindy Stevens, a former public-housing administrator, and Pege Gilgannon, a former photojournalist, who wore a shirt emblazoned with the words “Free D.C.” (She frequently volunteers for the D.C.-statehood movement.) Leading the group was Patti Curtis, a STEM adviser at the Department of Education, who retired just before its DOGE-driven evisceration. “They eliminated the entire research department,” she said. “I’m grateful that the Smithsonian isn’t just rolling over like some of our federal agencies.”

The four women are neighbors, and belong to a nonprofit community for seniors. “It’s your second family,” Gilgannon explained. “So you don’t just sit there playing mah-jongg.” Last summer, Curtis persuaded them to join Citizen Historians, a grassroots effort to monitor Smithsonian exhibitions for political interference. She’d heard about the group from one of its founders, James Millward, a central-Asia scholar at Georgetown. “He said, ‘I’ve taught in China and seen history erased, and I don’t want it to happen here.’ ” Not long before, Trump had pressured the director of the National Portrait Gallery, Kim Sajet, to resign, in part because his official portrait’s wall text mentioned his two impeachments. Curtis organized forty volunteers to photograph its collections; altogether, more than seven hundred people have participated in Citizen Historian campaigns.

Trump’s anti-Smithsonian crusade began in March, 2025, with an executive order called “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.” A declaration of war against a “revisionist movement” that saw America as “irredeemably flawed,” the order called for the removal of “improper ideology” from the Smithsonian’s twenty-one museums, and threatened to slash the institution’s funding if it didn’t comply. Soon, there were panicked reports—later debunked—that artifacts from slavery and the civil-rights movement had been quietly removed.

For a year, though, the Smithsonian has been spared, in part because of its semi-independent status. It’s governed by a seventeen-member Board of Regents, which includes the Vice-President, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, six federal lawmakers, and nine congressionally appointed members of the general public. The institution’s secretary, Lonnie G. Bunch III, has defended its integrity, but also shrewdly avoided provocative shows of resistance. Last August, he reportedly charmed Trump over lunch at the White House, and by the start of this summer’s Semiquincentennial celebrations, it was almost possible to believe that the Administration had moved on. Then, on July 4th, the White House Domestic Policy Council published a report called “Saving America’s Story,” which alleges that the N.M.A.H. has been hijacked by a cohort of radical activists. Shortly thereafter, Trump ordered the National Park Service to install warning signs outside the museum, whose director, Anthea Hartig, was summoned to testify on Capitol Hill.

“I was disturbed to hear about the quetzal,” Morgan Griffith, a congressman from Virginia, told Hartig, alluding to the suspiciously foreign bird feathers in a children’s show about money. (Quetzal feathers were once used as currency by the Aztecs and their trading partners in the American Southwest.) Nancy Mace, of South Carolina, called Hartig an ally of “queer pedophiles,” adducing, as evidence, a photo of RuPaul from an exhibition on American pop culture. Republicans also played a montage of Hartig making land acknowledgments, demanded to know why she’d once said that “loving America is very complicated,” and expressed outrage that no special exhibitions had been mounted about the Founding Fathers or the Declaration of Independence.

Democrats denounced the proceedings as a totalitarian show trial. Their star witness, the Pulitzer-winning historian David W. Blight, called the White House report “a declaration of political war on the historian’s profession,” and scoffed at accusations of left-wing revisionism. “All history is revision,” he said. “Would you prefer your doctors not to be revisionists?” Hartig, by contrast, was polite almost to the point of meekness, constrained by her role to “Sir”ing and “Ma’am”ing her inquisitors while affirming her commitment to a patriotism that was “not instructed but inspired.” She invited lawmakers to “walk the building with me” and “stand in front of the Star-Spangled Banner, in awe”—implying, not without reason, that many had never even visited the museum they were so determined to control.

If they did come, the Citizen Historians were determined to get there first. Curtis unfolded a map of the museum with eight galleries circled in hot pink. “We powwowed last night and realized we could hit four of them,” she explained. “Rather than split up, let’s go together and saturate.”

“Can anybody read that?” Gilgannon whispered, holding her phone up like a flashlight.

“Yeah, ‘Oh say can you see by the dawn’s early light,’ ” Curtis replied.

We were standing in the darkened chamber that houses the Star-Spangled Banner, whose tattered stripes were dimly visible behind glass. The flag was made by Mary Pickersgill, who sewed it with the help of her daughter, two nieces, and an “African-American indentured servant” named Grace Wisher. Curtis frowned. “Do we really think she was an ‘indentured servant’?” she asked, wondering if the label had originally read “slave.” Gilgannon sighed: “I hate how they put it in your head that you’re gonna get tricked.”

The White House report contends that N.M.A.H. has abandoned patriotism and erased the Founding Fathers in service of an “anti-white agenda” that seeks to “divide, dispirit, and discourage our citizens.” But a quick search of the collections database revealed that nearly a hundred objects associated with George Washington and the Revolutionary War—including Washington’s uniform, his battle sword, and his dinner plates—were on display. From the Star-Spangled Banner, we made our way to Horatio Greenough’s 1841 sculpture of a shirtless, sword-bearing Washington, its caption explaining how the sculptor had captured his “highest and noblest virtues.” Greenbush, the tour guide, was amused by his neoclassically bare chest. “He would have been mortified, I’m sure.”

Behind Washington was “Many Voices, One Nation,” an exhibition about the struggle of disparate peoples to forge an American identity. A video collage showcasing America’s diversity played on loop near the entrance; Gilgannon, whose family comes from Belgium, said, “My mother’s in there.” The four women fanned out to photograph the objects on display: an Irish brooch, a Chinese-American shop sign, a collection of accessories abandoned by migrants in the Sonoran Desert. The report frames the show as “pro-illegal alien activism,” but hadn’t mentioned its Border Patrol uniform, whose caption praised the agent’s twenty-two years of service. Later, we gawked at the lavishly decorated 1963 Chevy Impala in “Corazón y vida,” another exhibit derided as a paean to “foreign” peoples—the Chicanos of Southern California, who started building “lowriders” with elaborate hydraulic systems in the nineteen-forties. “I think I’d be scared when it lifts up,” Curtis said, inspecting the undercarriage. “We went to see ‘The Odyssey’ in 4DX a few weeks ago and I was screaming!”

On the top floor was “American Democracy,” a sweeping exhibition about self-governance. Near the entrance was the desk where Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence. Farther in was paraphernalia from a quarter millennium of Presidential campaigns, including Trump’s. (There was even a MAGA hat.) The exhibition culminated in a display of protest signs. The report characterizes them as “almost all for various progressive causes,” and I quickly spotted slogans familiar from Black Lives Matter and the campaign for marriage equality. But equally prominent were “Secure Our Borders,” “Stop Abortion Now,” and projected footage from a Tea Party rally—all unmentioned. Gilgannon took a picture of one from the D.C.-statehood movement. “They practice and promote joy,” she explained. “At first, I thought, What’s this crazy woo-woo? But that’s what’s going to bond us together when we have to, like, fight the National Guard.”

There was plenty of joy in “Entertainment Nation,” a bright, busy, and noisily media-rich survey of American pop culture. Greeting visitors was a photo of the jazz trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie, a “cool, Cold Warrior” who used music to fight Communism. Nearby was the sheet music for Irving Berlin’s “God Bless America” and Dorothy’s ruby slippers from “The Wizard of Oz,” whose L.G.B.T.Q. affiliations somehow escaped Republican scrutiny. It took several minutes for Greenbush and me to find the exhibition’s most controversial inclusion—an animation sketch depicting Mickey Mouse’s début in “Steamboat Willie” (1928), whose caption links the character to “longstanding traditions of blackface minstrelsy.” For once, a Citizen Historian and the report were on the same side. “Who would even make that connection?” Greenbush scoffed. “Maybe I’m naïve, but I never would have thought that. And there were points where I did watch a lot of Mickey Mouse.”

During the hearings, Representative Brandon Gill, of Texas, asked Hartig a question precision-engineered to extract a disqualifying sound bite: “Is Mickey Mouse racist?” When she said no, Gill quoted the caption—and again, Hartig affirmed Mickey’s innocence. “You don’t think blackface minstrelsy is racist?” Gill asked, now genuinely confused. Hartig kept calm. “It’s not for me to determine what’s problematic,” she replied. “It’s for me to determine what’s accurate.”

It’s well established that the Mickey Mouse of “Steamboat Willie”—who wears white gloves and performs the minstrel standard “Turkey in the Straw” on a paddle steamer—has its roots in blackface, which was, for nearly a century, one of America’s most popular forms of entertainment. To Republican lawmakers, pointing this out is character assassination, an attempt to cancel poor Mickey and all who hold him dear. But if Representative Gill visited the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American Culture, he might be surprised to learn how many great Black entertainers—including Eubie Blake and Josephine Baker—share Mickey’s checkered beginnings, and with what impartial curiosity these are explored.

Our tour of “Entertainment Nation” concluded with a video installation called “What’s So Funny?” It juxtaposed racist moments in old films and cartoons—Judy Garland dancing in blackface, Bugs Bunny fighting the Indian Wars—with excerpts from the routines of nonwhite comedians such as Margaret Cho and Richard Pryor. We laughed and cringed by turns, our faces painted by the light from the projectors. The 1946 film “Song of the South” came on, and I could feel us all torn between humming along to “Zip-A-Dee-Do-Dah”—a song that my grandmother, a Black woman, loves enough that she once bought an alarm clock with the melody—and recoiling in shame from Uncle Remus’s toothy grin. “My grandfather was actually in minstrel shows,” Greenbush abruptly volunteered. And yet, there she was, protecting our messy common heritage from being wiped clean.

How did the Smithsonian commemorate American history in simpler times, before postmodernism, intersectionality, and the many other Hydra heads of “woke”? The museum’s Semiquincentennial exhibitions struck me as neutral enough. But in order to assess their patriotism objectively, I needed to see how the N.M.A.H. had marked the 1976 Bicentennial, when the museum, the Smithsonian, and the federal government were all helmed by white men.

To my surprise, there was nary an exhibition dedicated to a Founding Father. But there had been a monumental show called “The Nation of Nations,” whose subject was America’s diversity. It opened with a survey of Native cultures, tracing the country’s identity as a “nation of immigrants” to the first Siberians who crossed the Bering Strait. A display about Ellis Island—which played recordings in dozens of languages—celebrated modern immigration, while a re-created nineteenth-century classroom was used to explain the process of naturalization. An entire section dedicated to American prejudice included anti-Japanese signage and a Ku Klux Klan hood.

Curators seem not to have worried that this would divide the American people. In the exhibition catalogue, then secretary of the Smithsonian S. Dillon Ripley—a former intelligence officer who was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by Ronald Reagan—describes America as “a place of turmoil among red men, white men, black men, and yellow men.” Yet no one hauled him before Congress to answer for stoking racial tensions, snubbing George Washington, or making America sad on her birthday. Today’s Smithsonian should be equally uncontroversial—and, without the Trump Administration’s propaganda, it probably would be.

The institution remains vulnerable. Republicans have proposed cutting its budget by more than ten per cent, and if they can fill the vacancies on its Board of Regents before the midterm elections, they may be able to fire Bunch. Yet there are also signs that the right’s revisionism panic might be petering out. Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska recently came out in support of the Smithsonian, while the Second Lady, Usha Vance, even feels comfortable collaborating with it. In May, she led a story-time event at the N.M.A.H. in honor of Asian American and Pacific Islander Heritage Month—in other words, a D.E.I. event for children, at a museum that her party believes is full of “inappropriate sexual and ideological content.” (She read from “Masala Chai, Fast and Slow,” by Rajani LaRocca, who is also known for “Some of Us,” a book for early readers that celebrates immigrant citizenship.)

She’s not the only conservative who didn’t get the memo. The day after my visit to the N.M.A.H., I went to see “America’s Presidents” at the National Portrait Gallery, where I found a father and son snapping selfies in front of Trump’s glowering mien. “We wanted to have a last weekend together before he went off to college,” the man explained; earlier, they’d been to the National Air and Space Museum. The man proudly acknowledged supporting Trump, but seemed confused when I asked if he’d spotted anything “radical.” He recalled a caption about a “wealthy landowner back in the day” who’d enslaved Native Americans, which he wasn’t sure was relevant, but he wouldn’t go so far as to say that it ought to be removed. “I don’t know if it’s unpatriotic,” he said. “It’s all good and bad. It’s part of our history.” ♦

Julian Lucas, a staff writer, began contributing to The New Yorker in 2018.

title: The Lantern of the Laughless Saint, a Morrowind-inspired RPG weirdfest out this week in early access, has immediately seduced me with dialogue camera hijinks
author: Mark Warren
content:
I want everything to do with this, madman

I've woken up on a beach. I'm staring up into the nostrils of a bald man whose face looks to be made of wet clay. He's saying vaguely threatening things about a tower and my race and an island and the fact I'm far from home. The dialogue camera of The Lantern of the Laughless Saint clearly picks up on how unnerved this introduction to its adventure has made me.

It pings back and forth between close-ups of my tortured visage - zooming in on my bald spot, brown moustache, and bright red eyes which are far too close together - and the equally weird face of the bloke interrogating me. At one point, it decides to look over his shoulder, but only keep focus on the bits of his cheek and neck which happen to be caught in the shot. The result's worthy of any spot a tech-averse old man's phone camera roll. My character, Bob, wants out of this chat. "I want nothing to do this, madman," he declares as the sun stings the beetroot pink streaks across his skin.

Eventually, the madman runs off to go and find a tower. Bob still can't let his guard down. The madman's gone, but the unhinged dialogue camera's still here. It's also crafty. It bides its time. Bob chats to various people around the starter town of Magdal's Rest. None of them activate the same dialogue camera as that first madman. Then...ARRRRRRRRRRRRRRRRRGGGGHHHHHHHHHHHHH.

1 of 4

Caption

Attribution

The merchant Pichess has activated it! It randomly decides to focus in on his ear as he hands Bob a quest to fetch some lost goods from the skeleton-infested road just outside of town. At least the quest earns Bob the key to a shack in town, somewhere he can shelter from the threat of camera ambushes and plan how he plans to tackle exploring the rest of the island. The latter will be saved for whenever I get time to play more than the first half an hour of The Lantern of the Laughless Saint.

Based on this small bite of it, most of which I spent giggling at freaky faces and wonky shots of them, it feels like a blend of stated inspiration Morrowind and Oblivion's brilliantly wacky Shivering Isles expansion. Mechanically, it's much more Morrowindy, but the tone of the island's loose community of eccentric cast-offs wouldn't feel out of place in Passwall or one of hamlets on the Mania side of Sheogorath's realm.

As such, NerveLabs' creation is a game I'll be keeping an eye on following its release in early access earlier this week. The devs are planning to update it every one or two weeks while it's in early access, and have it ready for a full release in less than a year. If you fancy wishlisting it, you can do so on Steam.

title: "Buying any of our games helps support the studio": Psychonauts studio Double Fine are the latest former Xbox-owned studio to get the rights to their games back
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
"We can turn that money into revenue that helps us extend that runway"

Earlier this week, South of Midnight developer Compulsion Games shared word that they now own all of the publishing rights to their games, a welcome update in light of the ongoing BDS boycott against Microsoft and Xbox. And now, another studio is joining the realm of boycott freedom, this time Psychonauts studio Double Fine, as CEO Tim Schafer has confirmed that they too now own the publishing rights to their own catalogue.

Speaking on Kinda Funny Games Daily (ta, Kotaku), Schafer said, "the transfer of the IP came back to us. We have the publishing rights back to our games. It still says ‘Microsoft’ on some of them, but it just takes a while for it all to process. When people buy our games, it supports the studio. So if you’re curious, buying any of our games helps support the studio, and we can turn that money into revenue that helps us extend that runway."

That's not the only spot of good news, as Double Fine are planning to bring back their Amnesia Fortnight Game Jam. "Being independent again, we can go back to do a lot of things we were doing before. Like crazy game jams, like our Amnesia Fortnight Game Jam where we split into small groups and we make a game in two weeks…Game jams and, you know, we got a little bit of runway on the departure to sign some games. We want to sign some game deals, get going, it’s kind of a scary time to be out there. It’s a runway, not a freeway, it doesn’t go forever. It’s just a little patch where we can take off on our own power, and we want to extend it a little bit."

In fact, the studio is hosting a Kickstarter for the return of this game jam, which kicks off August 31st. As Schafer explains, "if you join the Kickstarter, you get to vote, you get to hear all the teams pitch. Everyone at Double Fine gets to pitch a game. And if you join that, you get to help vote for which one we actually make, and we’ll make like four of them, and then you get to vote on which one we [work on] for a little bit longer to polish up and actually release."

As nice as it is to see Double Fine return to their indie roots, this does unfortunately come a month after they laid off a quarter of their staff, which obviously came as a result of their independence from Xbox. Hopefully those devs manage to land on their feet, and the remaining devs at Double Fine continue to keep the lights on.

title: Total War: Warhammer 3 is getting a big free vampiric update in September, alongside the epithet-stuffed Lords of the End Times DLC
author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
content:
TOD! *clang* BRINGER! *clang*

Creative Assembly have announced a release date for Total War: Warhammer 3 expansion Lords of the End Times. Consisting of four new legendary lords, each with a distinct retinue, campaign and battle map abilities, it's billed as "the biggest DLC that we’ve ever released in the series 10-year history". It'll accompany another, reportedly gargantuan free update with yet another legendary lord, the Vampire Queen Neferata, together with a rework for the Vampire Counts and Archaon The Everchosen, some new endgame scenarios, and updated victory conditions.

There are over a hundred legendary lords in Twarhammer 3 at this point. I feel like the legendariness is at risk of being diluted. Can we organise some kind of spin-off game where every Warhammer army consists entirely of legendary lords? How about the legendary lords all go live on a big New England college campus and solve mysteries together? How about a Warhammer legendary lord adaptation of Guess Who?

The new expansion's star is Nagash, necromancer supreme, who's out to collect magic books and gather his Mortarch lieutenants so that he can reign over a world of dusty bones. To do that, he'll have to outmanoeuvre new skaven legendary lord Thanquol, aka the grey seer, who rides around on a rat ogre and can enact masterplans, such as heists and evil rituals, to sabotage opponents. As is the way of mega rodent initiatives, these masterplans do occasionally backfire.

The Empire have a new elector count, who rejoices in the name of Boris Todbringer. He will Bring the Tod to any and all enemies of the wolftod wolfgod Ulric. Defeat enemies, and you'll raise fervor that is used to build a big wolf temple, enhance its sanctuaries and perform winter rites that make your armies better at killing stuff. Boris also has a sword called Legbiter, which I assume can be used on body parts besides legs.

But will that be enough to see off the Glottkin, Befouled Brothers of the Chaos god Nurgle? These lads excel at spreading corruption, turning settlements into plague gardens that give them access to "a higher proportion of Daemonic Nurgle units than any other Warriors of Chaos faction". There are three of the Befouled Brothers – one wields a scythe, another a staff, and they both ride around the shoulders of the third. I do love Nurgle bodymodding. All those extra mouths and tentacles jammed into every spare inch of skin. It's like when too many kids try to decorate an Xmas tree.

All this will hit your plate on 24th September. Again, I can't say I think Total War: Warhammer 3 particularly needs any extra people or things right now. You can barely move for Boar Boyz and Phoenix Guards already. I'm more interested in the forthcoming Total War: Warhammer 40,000, which appears to be dropping an Exterminatus on a few long-standing Total War conventions.

title: What are we all playing this weekend?
author: Julian Benson
content:
Well? Do tell!

For the past ten days or so I've been whinging my way through a chest infection. My partner's been sent out for lemsips, tissues, the blood of a vital youth filled with hopes of a bright future, and chicken soup. With the last dregs of the lurgy coming out of me in runs of coughs I'm starting to feel well again, meaning I've a weekend of ignored chores to catch up on. That and attending a one-year-old's birthday party.

Fingers crossed my immune system is now in fighting form because, with Gamescom next week, it would be right annoying to pick up something else.

But enough about me, what's the rest of the team up to this weekend?

OllieThis weekend it looks like I'll be playing the wonderful game of sitting in bed nursing a pint of hot honey, lemon, and ginger, and hoping that my coughing fits start to calm down long enough for me to sleep. Yep, I'm feeling just dandy at the moment! On the offchance I do get some energy to go downstairs, I'll probably end up playing more Mortal Shell 2 for our walkthrough.

JamesI needed a holiday after playing nothing but STALKER 2 for weeks. I'll be back on Monday, refreshed and ready to squeeze in some STALKER 2 before Gamescom.

Mark(inhales) SECRET GAME, BE VERY QUIET. THIS IS JUST BETWEEN US, YEAH?

EdwinThis weekend I'll be melting mountain ice caps in Sandustry to supply my gold-panning operation with fresh water. I'm also feeling the need to play CleanFall, an equally vertigo-inducing game about a robomaid who cobbles together huge, sloppy airships in order to fly to the bottom of Hell.

JeremyMore Mortal Shell 2 for me this weekend. You all read my review, didn't you? Despite the occasional bugs and bouts of jank, it's a good game, and I'm glad to see it doing well despite the Soulslike subreddit trying to tell me that actually, the hype is too much and it's mid. Excuse me, I need to go get my Axetana (that's an axe-katana hybrid, a real thing that exists in this game) to go run through some goons.

CallumWhatever Callum is up to it best not be sneaking food to the people in the pit. Callum wouldn't do that, now would he? He has, after all, been warned.

JulianAfter hearing Edwin big up the sand game in the morning meeting, I played some over lunch on Friday. Promptly forgot lunch was supposed to end after an hour and kept playing for another hour afterward. So, I will be returning to scratch that itch throughout the weekend. (When not attending a one-year-old's birthday party.)

And you, reader dear, what are you playing this weekend…?

title: Invisum Piscium 嫌魚 is a dreamlike walking sim about fragments of conversations and a deep craving for water fish haven't procreated in
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
You know, the regular stuff

I won't dive into why this is happening to me at the moment, you'll either need to pay me £20 or let me pay you to be my therapist to get that explanation, but I've been having some odd dreams lately. They're frequently temporally confused, mixing and matching people from across my life that should never have crossed paths. This has left me looking to ground myself a touch, so of course I decided to take a look at Invisum Piscium 嫌魚, a walking sim that's not quite about dreaming, but is about looking for distilled water that's free from fish sex contamination.

Invisum Piscium 嫌魚 is upfront about what it is on its Steam page. Atmosphere and exploration come first, there are "almost no traditional puzzle elements," you can pick up items and use them to "subtly alter the world." There's no question about this in the demo either. It opens in a bathroom, a rubber duck in front of you on the side of the bath. Of course you interact with the rubber duck, and it speaks back to you.

You leave the bathroom and find the main room in the apartment, a woman that looks like a plush doll brought to life starts talking to you about how she's losing her mind over the fact that fish mate in water, so she's feeling anxious about drinking it and asks for some distilled water. The quest begins! What follows in the demo, the process of getting to its ending (which does not see you acquire the distilled water) reminds me of the trading sequence in Link's Awakening, albeit in a smaller scale.

A depressed goth with a cat plush gives you a cake. She feels empty. You give the cake to a bunny girl, and she explodes and dies, so you bring her back to life with an energy drink. You find some money, so you buy a snack, and give it to the goth, and the exchange of miscellaneous goods continues. Ghosts float around the apartment complex you find yourself in with the goth and bunny girl, spouting cryptic messages. In the distance you can see the clouds, the corners of the skybox as clear as day and you wonder what the limits of this world are.

The demo for Invisum Piscium 嫌魚 isn't all that long, and it's not clear how big the full game would be. It certainly feels like it sits in conversation with indie classic Yume Nikki, and more recent games like nophenia. How far we'll all be lulled into its dreamlike world is a question that's yet to be answered. You can check out Invisum Piscium 嫌魚 for yourself on Steam.

title: Horizon Hunters Gathering is reportedly being rebooted without its live service bits following negative playtest feedback
author: Connor Makar
content:
Avad nother try.

Horizon Hunters Gathering has reportedly been rebooted in order to ditch its live service elements, following negative feedback during early private playtests.

Per a new report from Jason Schreier at Bloomberg, sources "familiar with the company's plans" claim developer Guerilla Games has been overhauling Horizon Hunters Gathering into more of a traditional multiplayer co-op game since June, in response to poor playtester feedback. As a result, all the live service mechanics are being stripped out in favour of a story mode and a "far smaller scope."

Bloomberg reports that while the game has not yet been cancelled, Guerilla Games has until December to impress PlayStation bosses. In addition, many of the Hunter Gathering developers are being reassigned to another project at the studio, which is also being evaluated by executives at the end of the year.

This marks yet another setback for Sony's live service aspirations, which have been continuously challenged over the past few years.

Concord, the most famous of its live service failures, was shut down and taken off storefronts soon after its release. There's also been a string of live service project cancellations at PlayStation. Bluepoint Games was shuttered after a God of War live service game was cancelled; Naughty Dog's Last of Us multiplayer game was killed too, reportedly when it was 80 percent complete, and a Twisted Metal battle royale game got the chop a few years ago. Meanwhile, there's Marathon's ongoing underperformance and the strangely silent Fairgames, which lost its director last year.

It's safe to say, it's not been a particularly easy few years for Sony as it hunts for a live service mega hit. Here's hoping the good people at Guerilla Games can turn Horizon Hunter Gathering into something the higher-ups are happy with.

title: Action RPG juggernaut Path of Exile 2 finally has its 1.0 release date and it's coming this year, at which point it becomes free-to-play
author: Sherif Saed
content:
At Wraeclast.

Grinding Gear Games made a surprise Path of Exile 2 announcement at Gamescom Opening Night Live yesterday. The developer confirmed when the game's long-awaited 1.0 release will be.

Path of Exile 2 leaves early access 11th December, which is also when the game will be available as a free-to-play game, dropping the nominal charge for the Founder's Pack requirement it currently has - the only way into the early access version.

The 1.0 release introduces a new class in the Duelist, a melee-focused character and strangely the game's first sword-wielding class. The Duelist can also use shields and is designed for aggressive combat. The two remaining campaign Acts will also be part of the 1.0 launch, completing the campaign.

Grinding Gear is running a free registration campaign from now until the launch on the official Path of Exile website. The more players that sign up, the more rewards can be unlocked for the entire community, including a pet.

The Path of Exile 2 full release arrives almost exactly two years after the initial early access launch. The 1.0 date has been something of a moving target, though the developer did say earlier this year that it's aiming to launch it sometime after November's ExileCon Path of Exile convention.

The early access release, which notably included PlayStation and Xbox, has been successful, with long queue times as millions jumped in on day one. Eurogamer's Robert Purchese spoke highly of the game's quality in their early access review, in particular praising its challenging Souls-y approach to combat that rewards perseverance and sets it apart from other high-quality ARPGS.

title: What’s the Secret to Bats’ Super Longevity? - Nautilus
content:
Bats are exceptional for a number of reasons. But two in particular stand out. First, the largest genus of bats, Myotis, can carry up to hundreds of viruses without ever getting sick. Second, they have impressive lifespans relative to their body size—as much as 42 years in the case of the minuscule Brandt’s bat (M. brandtii).

Featured Video

A study published today in Nature by an international collaboration of biologists explored Myotis genes to better understand both their pathogen-resistance and their longevity. “These are often studied as separate biological problems,” explained co-lead study author Elise Lauterbur, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Vermont, in a press release. “But our results suggest that evolution may be shaping them together.”

Read more: “The Social Life of Bats”

The researchers sampled tissue from eight closely related Myotis species from the American West. Using a no-kill technique pioneered by co-lead study author Juan Manuel “Manny” Vazquez, a biologist at Penn State University, they biopsied circular patches from the bat wings. From those, they grew cell lines, from which they extracted nearly complete genomes and identified genes related to lifespan, cancer-resistance, and virus tolerance. They focused on the gene “protein kinase t” that’s known to serve in immunity in all mammals. 

The results revealed that bats have one or two extra copies of this key gene, in contrast to the single copy known from other mammals. The gene appears to play a protective role in preventing cell damage. Case in point: In cells of little brown bats (M. lucifugus), the gene helped cope when a pox virus was introduced to the cell line. Damaged cells were either repaired or discarded entirely.

“The little brown bats start committing to kill off cells,” said Vazquez. “Our hypothesis is (that) it’s dumping the cells that can’t be salvaged.”

In other words, bats have a distinct way of handling viruses that’s not seen in other mammals. They survive pathogens through a genomic response that also confers cancer-resistance and therefore longevity. Further understanding how this remarkably diverse genus, comprising at least 139 species, acquired its disease-resistance could curb zoonotic disease transmission—and maybe help all of us live a little bit longer, too.

title: Melon’s Odyssey On The Black Market For Life-Saving Cat Medicine
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
When Sabrina Imbler’s cat, Melon, becomes seriously ill with what is later confirmed as feline infectious peritonitis (FIP), Imbler feels she doesn’t have time to wait for a formal diagnosis and turns to a Facebook group that connects desperate cat owners with a black‑market treatment: GS‑441524. Injecting Melon twice a day at home, they enter a frantic stretch in which the acidic drug causes a wound to open on Melon’s back, and she is sentenced to weeks in a hated recovery suit called a Suitical: “Melon was so upset that she lay on her side like a tipped cow for hours, her chin glumly fixed to the carpet.” With Melon finally fully recovered, Imbler has the space to look back on the desperate measures it took to save her.

The FIP Warriors contact met me in the lobby of their building, wearing a knit cap with cat ears. They proceeded to demonstrate how to deliver the medicine on their stuffed cat, Edward. I watched as they manipulated the stuffed toy, lifting up pockets in Edward’s “skin” into which I was to drive a 22-gauge needle at an angle into subcutaneous tissue. I paid $50 for two vials of injectable GS-441524, which was acidic to keep it shelf-stable. This acidity, the contact warned me, meant the injections burned. “It’s really best if you have help,” they told me. “Will you have help?” No, I told them. My ex was out of town and it was just me and Melon. “Well, you’ll figure something out,” they said. I would have to.
